content: The Victorian College of Pharmacy serves as the Parkville campus of Monash University, located in Victoria, Australia. It is a prominent institution for research and education in the fields of pharmaceuticals and medicinal chemistry. The college is particularly renowned for its contributions to drug development and formulation science, including the discovery and development of Relenza, the world’s first successful anti-influenza drug. The campus comprises four buildings, with the most recent one being occupied in 2007. This newest building is primarily dedicated to research, aligning with the college’s strong emphasis on research activities. The campus is situated on Royal Parade in the suburb of Parkville, approximately 2 kilometers north of Melbourne’s central business district. Royal Parade is also home to several other research institutions, such as the University of Melbourne, the CSIRO’s Division of Health Sciences, and the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Additionally, the pharmaceutical company CSL Limited is based in Parkville. The college offers undergraduate courses in Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Science, which are highly competitive and require high ENTER scores from Year 12 applicants. Students at the College of Pharmacy can also pursue dual degrees in commerce or engineering at Monash University’s Clayton campus. Postgraduate degrees are available through coursework or research, ranging from graduate diplomas to PhD programs. The college currently has approximately 1,100 students and 140 staff members. Plans are underway to expand its teaching offerings, including the introduction of a Bachelor of Pharmacy program at Monash University’s Malaysia campus, set to commence in 2008. The college is also exploring the development of postgraduate pharmacy education at Monash University’s South Africa campus. The official faculty color of the College of Pharmacy is a shade of light green. The current Dean of the college is Professor Bill Charman. History The Victorian College of Pharmacy is one of Australia’s oldest educational institutions, established in 1881 as the School of the Pharmaceutical Society of Victoria. After being housed in various locations in Melbourne, it moved to its current site in 1960. In its early years, the college operated as a private institution, with most of its funding derived from tuition fees and donations from benefactors. In 1967, the college entered into an agreement with the Federal and State governments to receive government financial assistance. In 1974, tertiary education fees in Australia were abolished, leading to the college’s funding being primarily sourced from the Federal Government. Following the introduction of the unified national system of higher education in 1988, known as the Dawkins reforms, it became evident that the college needed to merge with a university. Initial negotiations with the University of Melbourne, considered a logical partner due to its proximity, failed in 1990. Subsequently, discussions with Monash University were successful, and the transfer was finalized on July 1, 1992. The college is now the Faculty of Pharmacy at Monash University. It celebrated its 125th anniversary in 2006. Deans and Directors John Kruse (1882–1885) Cuthbert Blackett (1886) (acting) Alfred H. S. ‘Stan’ Sissons (1920–1962) Nigel Manning (1963–1978) Geoffrey Vaughan (1979–1987) Robert Burnet (1987) (acting) Colin Raper (1987) (acting) Tom R. Watson (1988–1991) Colin Chapman (1991–2006) Bill Charman (2007–present) Structure The college’s teaching structure includes the following departments: Department of Medicinal Chemistry Department of Pharmaceutical Biology and Pharmacology Department of Pharmaceutics Department of Pharmacy Practice The college also hosts research centers, such as the Centre for Drug Candidate Optimisation. Notable Alumni The Victorian College of Pharmacy has produced numerous graduates who have become leaders in pharmaceutical and health sciences. Additionally, its alumni include individuals who have achieved prominence in fields outside of science, such as politics, senior public service, and national leadership. Notable figures include Weary Dunlop.
